To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

people often believe that they are better at learning than they actually are, they often fail to recognize the importance of effort in learning and remembering, and they often overestimate how much they will learn and remember from studying.

people have a faulty mental models of how they learn; this mental model can be improved by training; people's ongoing assessments are influenced by current and fluency; and these ongoing assessments can be improved by metacognitive training.
people's beliefs and strategies for self-regulated learning are often not well aligned with the actual mechanisms that govern learning and remembering.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how people think they learn and with how they monitor and manage their own learning, and how these processes can be enhanced to promote more effective learning and performance.
the question of what people need to understand in terms of their own learning in order to become maximally effective in managing that learning.
how people think about learning and with how their beliefs and assumptions about learning can affect their ability to manage their own learning effectively.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
self-regulated learning is a process that is not yet fully understood, but that it is a process that can be learned and improved through training and education.

self-regulated learning is a complex and multifaceted construct that has received considerable attention from a variety of disciplines and perspectives, and that the research on this construct has been growing rapidly in the past decade.

people's beliefs about how they learn are often inaccurate, that their self-assessments are often biased, that their self-regulated learning techniques often do not match their needs or goals, and that their illusions about learning often lead them to adopt ineffective learning strategies.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the most effective learners have a realistic mental model of how learning works, are motivated to learn and to improve, are able to assess their learning accurately, and have the self-regulatory abilities necessary to manage their learning effectively.
people are often unaware of their own limitations and are prone to overestimating their own abilities, and that this tendency is exacerbated in situations in which they feel confident and competent.

the research literature on self-regulated learning has provided strong evidence that learners need to understand how their own learning is influenced by a number of factors that are not under their conscious control and that learners are prone to misassessing the quality of their learning.
The main takeaway from our work is that
people are not as good at self-regulating their own learning as they might like to think they are.
people are often poor judges of how they learn.

the most important aspect of self-regulated learning is not the use of particular techniques, but rather the beliefs and attitudes that people have about their own learning and the learning process in general.
